aperture: The group of pixels whose light is added up to make a star's light curve. Choosing it well keeps the star's light in and the neighbours' light out. See Chapter 3.
arcsecond: A tiny angle: 1/3,600 of a degree. A TESS pixel covers 21 arcseconds. Written ″; an arcminute (′) is 60 of them. See Chapter 1.
binary-star: Two stars held together by gravity, each circling their shared centre. Our hunting ground: pairs where a planet might orbit both. See Chapter 4.
biweight-filter: A way to draw a smooth line through a light curve that ignores dips and outliers, so slow trends can be divided out without erasing a transit. Our detector uses a 2-day one. See Chapter 7.
btjd: The TESS clock, in days: Barycentric Julian Date minus 2,457,000. BTJD 4025.6 is 16 December 2025.
cadence: One measurement in a light curve, or the time between measurements: 2 minutes for SPOC light curves, 200 seconds for today's full-frame images.
candidate: A dip in a light curve that passed our first checks and might be a planet. Not a planet until professionals confirm it.
cdpp: "Combined Differential Photometric Precision": NASA's estimate of how much a star's brightness wobbles over a given time (like 1 hour), stored in each light-curve file. See Chapter 7.
centroid: The centre of a star's light on the camera, like the balance point of its pixels. If it shifts during a dip, the dip may come from a neighbour. See Chapter 10.
circumbinary-planet: A planet that orbits both stars of a pair. Its dips come at irregular times, which is why standard searches miss them. Our main quest.
common-moment: A flag from version 7. A dip is doubtful if three or more other stars on the same camera have an event of either kind (a dip or an upside-down dip) within 0.1 days. It replaced the older burst flag, which counted only upside-down events and so treated the control differently from the data. See Chapter 8.
completeness: The share of real planets a search would catch, measured by hiding fake planets in real data and counting how many come back. Ours keeps about 83 in 100 strong ones through the flags. See Chapter 9.
control: A test run where the right answer is known to be "nothing", to see how many false alarms the method makes. Ours is the upside-down light curve. See Chapter 7.
critical-orbit: The closest a planet can orbit a pair of stars and stay stable: usually 2.5 to 3.5 times the stars' separation. See Chapter 4.
ctoi: Community TESS Object of Interest: a planet candidate found by a team outside NASA, posted on ExoFOP. See Chapter 1.
depth: How much of the star's light a dip blocks, as a fraction: depth = (planet radius ÷ star radius)². Usually given in % or ppm.
detached-binary: Two stars far enough apart that they don't touch or distort each other; their eclipses look like clean, separate dips. Our G1 list keeps only these (Kepler's "morph" value below 0.5).
detrending: Removing slow drifts (from the star or the spacecraft) so short dips stand out. We divide by a smooth fitted curve with a 2-day window. See Chapter 8.
dominated: A dip is dominated when the strongest upside-down dip in the same light curve is at least as strong. A fair local contest, with no setting to tune. See Chapter 8.
eclipse-overlap: A flag for a dip that falls inside one of the two stars' own eclipses, where it is the stars and not a planet. See Chapter 8.
eclipsing-binary: Two stars orbiting each other, lined up so that one passes in front of the other. Makes deep, regular dips.
exofop: The website where astronomers share follow-up information on TESS planet candidates. Since 2026 it asks for a published paper before accepting a community candidate. See Chapter 14.
false-alarm: A "detection" caused by noise or spacecraft effects instead of a real dip. We count them by searching upside-down data.
fits: The standard file format of astronomy since 1981: a header of labels plus tables or images. Every TESS file is FITS. See Lab 2.
flag: A reason to doubt a dip. We flag and sort dips, we never delete them. See Chapter 8.
flat-baseline-test: A transit is a box: the light just before and after it is normal. A dip whose two sides are not level, or that has no data on one side, is a ramp, a cliff or a data edge. Also called the step test. See Chapter 8.
frozen-settings: Every setting and a fingerprint of every file written down before any result is read, so the rules cannot be tuned to the answer. See Chapter 8.
full-frame-image-ffi: A picture of a TESS camera's whole view, saved every 30 minutes, 10 minutes or 200 seconds depending on the year. Every star in view is in it. See Chapter 3.
gaia: The European Space Agency's star-mapping spacecraft. Its catalogue gives positions, distances and colours for over a billion stars. See Chapter 1.
heavy-tails: Real noise makes far more very big wobbles than bell-curve noise would, so a 7 sigma dip is not as rare as the maths says. See Chapter 7.
injection-test: Hiding computer-made planet dips of known size in real data and checking how many the search finds. It measures what we can and can't detect.
kepler: NASA's space telescope that stared at one patch of sky from 2009 to 2013 and found thousands of planets and eclipsing binaries. Our G1 stars come from its binary catalogue. See Chapter 1.
kic: Kepler Input Catalog number: Kepler's ID for a star, like KIC 12644769 for Kepler-16.
light-curve: A star's brightness measured again and again over time and drawn as a graph: time along the bottom, brightness up the side.
look-elsewhere-effect: If you search in thousands of places, a few will show something unusual by chance. A search's false-alarm rate must count all its tries. See Chapter 7.
lopsided-noise: Noise that is not the same upwards and downwards: flares and glitches jump up more than down, so an upside-down light curve makes more false dips than a real one. See Chapter 7.
magnitude: Astronomy's brightness scale, where bigger numbers are fainter. 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100. See Chapter 1.
mast: The Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes: NASA's public archive holding all TESS and Kepler data. See Lab 1.
matched-filter: Sliding a template shaped like the signal you want (for us, a box-shaped dip) along the data and scoring how well each stretch matches.
momentum-dump: A short thruster firing that TESS uses every few days to stay pointed. It jolts the camera and can fake a dip; it's flagged in the data (quality bit 32). See Lab 2.
n-body-simulation: A computer calculation that moves several objects (like two stars and a planet) step by step under each other's gravity. STANLEY uses one to predict when a two-star planet crosses.
orbit-start-ramp: TESS settles and scattered light is strongest just after it resumes recording, which fakes slow dips. We doubt every dip within 1 day after data resumes. See Chapter 8.
parsec: A distance of about 3.26 light years, used by astronomers. Kepler-16 is 75 parsecs away.
pdcsap-and-sap: Two versions of NASA's light curves. SAP is the raw light summed in the star's pixels; PDCSAP has known spacecraft effects removed.
phase-fold: Cutting a light curve into pieces one period long and stacking them, so repeating events (like eclipses) line up. Our eclipse mask finds eclipses this way.
photon-noise: The natural wobble in counting particles of light: like raindrops in a bucket, a count of N varies by about √N. It's the floor no instrument can beat. See Chapter 7.
ppm: Parts per million. 1% = 10,000 ppm. Earth crossing the Sun blocks about 84 ppm.
precession: The slow turning of a planet's orbit around a pair of stars. It makes transits switch on and off over years. See Chapter 5.
qlp: MIT's Quick-Look Pipeline: makes light curves from full-frame images for a huge number of stars. All 549 G1 stars have QLP data. See Chapter 3.
quality-flag: A number stored with each measurement that warns about problems (thruster firing, scattered light...). 0 means fine. See Lab 2.
ra-and-dec: The sky's longitude (Right Ascension) and latitude (Declination). Every star's address. See Chapter 1.
radius: Distance from the centre of a star or planet to its edge. We measure planets in Earth radii and stars in Sun radii (the Sun is about 109 Earths wide).
red-noise: Slow wobbles where neighbouring measurements move together. Unlike random noise, it doesn't shrink much when you average, so it fakes planet-like dips. See Chapter 7.
repeater: A star with three or more dips in one sector. A planet around two stars cannot make that many in 27 days, so it is a variable star or a second eclipsing pair. See Chapter 10.
robust-spread: A measure of wobble that ignores a few wild points: 1.4826 times the median distance from the median. Our detector uses it everywhere. See Chapter 7.
scattered-light: Sunlight bounced off Earth or the Moon into TESS's cameras, raising the background. It creates slow ramps and fake dips, usually near the ends of each orbit.
secondary-eclipse: When the brighter star passes in front of the fainter one: a shallower dip than the primary eclipse, at another point in the binary's orbit.
sector: One TESS stretch of about 27 days looking at the same patch of sky.
snr: Signal-to-noise ratio: how big a signal is compared with normal wobble. SNR 7 means seven times the normal wobble. Our detection bar is 7.
spoc: NASA's Science Processing Operations Center: makes the cleanest TESS light curves, from 2-minute postage stamps. See Chapter 3.
stability-limit: The closest a planet can orbit a pair of stars without being thrown out, about 3.7 binary periods for equal stars. See Chapter 8.
stanley: A search tool by David Martin's group (Martin et al. 2021) that looks for two-star planets by simulating orbits and stacking all their predicted crossings together. Installed on your PC.
tess: NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018. It photographs most of the sky, one sector at a time. All its data is free.
tic: TESS Input Catalog number: TESS's ID for a star, like TIC 299096355 for Kepler-16. See Chapter 1.
tier: A bin for a dip after our flags: 1A, 1L and 1B are the unflagged ones (candidates could only come from there), tier 2 is flagged, tier 3 disagrees with a second data product. See Chapter 8.
toi: TESS Object of Interest: a signal NASA's team thinks might be a planet. TOI-1338 became TOI-1338 b once confirmed.
transit: A planet passing in front of its star as seen from Earth, which makes a small dip in the light curve.
virtual-environment: A private copy of Python with its own toolkits, kept inside a project folder so it doesn't clash with anything else. Ours is D:\second-sun\.venv. See Lab 0.
white-noise: Random wobble where each measurement is independent. Averaging N measurements shrinks it by √N. See Chapter 7.
